The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Cleveland, Ohio, I'm Dale Willman.
President Trump is expected to hit the campaign trail
in the Midwest on Sunday.
He'll be in both Iowa and Kansas.
They each have competitive races for governor and U.S. Senate.
NPR's Stephen Fowler reports on the final campaign push.
The president is holding his final in-person rallies of the midterms
in two states he won decisively in 2024,
but now have a lot of voters unhappy with his agenda.
His first stop, Dubuque, Iowa, in the second congressional district
that Trump won by double digits,
but now is on the edge of the competitive map.
Then Trump goes to Kansas, where polls show Republicans
could take control of the governor's office,
but lose the Senate race in another heavily conservative state.
Both parties are spending hundreds of millions of dollars
in these last few days to get out the vote
with a larger than usual number of House and Senate races
expected to be close.
Stephen Fowler, NPR News.
A group of former leaders of the U.S. Census Bureau
are now speaking out against the Trump administration's proposal
for unprecedented changes to the next census.
The plan would reshape voting maps
and how federal funding is distributed across the country.
And Piers Hanse LeWong has more on our story.
Three former Census Bureau directors
and three former acting directors are warning
the Trump administration's proposed changes
could risk the accuracy of the 2030 census.
The proposal calls for excluding millions of U.S. residents
from a key census count that, according to the 14th amendment,
must include the "whole number of persons" in each state
and counties used to determine each state's share
of congressional seats and electoral college votes
for a decade.
The Trump administration argues that constitution's framers
did not intend for the word "persons" to include people
living in the states without U.S. citizenship or a green card.
Trump officials also propose cutting questions
about race and ethnicity because they see a "reduced need"
for that information, which is used
for civil rights enforcement.
Public comments are due Monday.
Hanse LeWong, NPR News.
Iran's Supreme Leader says that his country will respond
forcefully if anyone attacks.
News of his comments comes, as the U.S. and Israel say
they're preparing for a potential return to hostilities
after the midterm elections next week.
Ampere's Hadil El-Shalchi has more on that story.
Ayatollah Mushta-Bahamane said that "any level or type of threat
to Iran would face a 'immediate and impactful response.'"
The Supreme Leader made the comments in a meeting
with Iranian military officials,
according to Iranian state media.
He also ordered the military to update their attack plans
with U.S. and Israeli targets.
This comes at a time when Iran has intensified its attacks
on ships trying to cross the Strait of Hormuz.
According to Iranian state media,
the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said that on Friday,
four tankers, one of which was carrying two million barrels
of oil, caught fire after hitting mines in the strait.
Hadil El-Shalchi, NPR News, Istanbul.
And this is NPR News.
Russia's oldest independent newspaper
says it's closing down due to intense state pressure.
As NPR's Charles Maynes reports,
it's the latest blow to independent Russian media
during the war in Ukraine.
For more than 30 years, Novik Gizeta reflected
the pro-democratic ideals of a post-Soviet Russia
that mostly fell short of them.
The newspaper was often critical of the Kremlin,
even as that reporting came at a cost.
Several of its journalists, including star investigative
reporter Anna Politkovsky, were murdered over their work.
Novik Gizeta's then editor-in-chief, Dmitry Murata,
was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021
over the paper's defense of press freedoms.
Yet in announcing the closing of staff statements
that amid the war in Ukraine,
the Kremlin had intentionally killed the paper's ability
to survive financially or report without its journalists
violating strict wartime censorship laws.
Charles Maynes, NPR News.
The National Weather Service says more heavy rains
in the southwestern U.S. this weekend
will bring a renewed threat of flash floods.
The region is still recovering from earlier flooding
as much as four inches of rain is expected into Monday,
and weather officials say because the ground
is already saturated, it won't take too much
to create major problems.
Number one, Miami survived a scare Saturday
when they slipped past unranked North Carolina, 38 to 35.
Number two, Ohio State struggled offensively
and a 30 to 18 loss to USC.
Defending champion Indiana needed overtime
to pull off a 23 to 16 win over Minnesota.
Number six, Utah beat Cincinnati 49 to 25,
UCLA blanked Nevada 27 to nothing,
and Chicago State beat Fort Lauderdale Eagles 80 to 17.
I'm Dale Willman, NPR News.
